Content:
A Turing machine is similar to a deterministic finite automaton. However, it is not finite because it has an associated tape of infinite length split into cells, and data may be read and written to the tape, one cell at a time. It is a universal machine, acting as an acceptor or a transducer depending on the setup.

Content:
More formally, a Turing machine is a seven-tuple of the form [MATH: T=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,q_1,q_0,\square,\delta),] where

Content:

- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols,
- [MATH: \Gamma] is a finite set of tape symbols with [MATH: \Sigma \subseteq \Gamma,]
- [MATH: q_1 \in Q] is the start state,
- [MATH: q_0] is the final or accepting state,
- [MATH: \square \in \Gamma \setminus \Sigma] is the blank cell symbol, representing an empty cell on the tape, and
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta : Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L,R\}.]

Content:
The function [MATH: \delta] takes the current state [MATH: q] and current tape symbol [MATH: X] and returns a state [MATH: q,] a tape symbol [MATH: Y,] and a direction [MATH: D,] either left ([MATH: L]) or right ([MATH: R]).

sections.normalized_html:
A Turing machine is a seven-tuple of the form [MATH: T = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, q_1, q_0, \square, \delta),] where

  • [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states,

  • [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols,

  • [MATH: \Gamma] is a finite set of tape symbols with [MATH: \Sigma \subseteq \Gamma,]

  • [MATH: q_1 \in Q] is the start state,

  • [MATH: q_0] is the final or accepting state,

  • [MATH: \square \in \Gamma \setminus \Sigma] is the blank cell symbol, and

  • [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta: Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{ L, R \}.]

The arguments of [MATH: \delta] are a state and a tape symbol currently scanned by the tape head. The function returns a new state, a new tape symbol replacing the old symbol in the scanned cell, and the direction in which the head moves ([MATH: L] stands for "left" and [MATH: R] stands for "right").

With that in mind, let's examine our diagram.

  • Consider the cell at the intersection of row [MATH: q_1] and column [MATH: {\color{red}0}.] In the diagram, this corresponds to the loop from [MATH: q_1] to [MATH: q_1,] labeled by [MATH: {\color{red}0}/1,L.]

    This means that being in state [MATH: q_1] and observing symbol [MATH: {\color{red}0}] in a cell, we stay in state [MATH: q_1,] write down [MATH: 1] into the cell, and move left. So, [MATH: \delta(q_1,0) = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(q_1,1,L)}.]

  • Consider the cell at the intersection of row [MATH: q_1] and column [MATH: {\color{red}\square}.] In the diagram, this corresponds to the arrow from [MATH: q_1] to [MATH: q_0,] labeled by [MATH: {\color{red}\square}/0,R.]

    This means that being in state [MATH: q_1] and observing an empty cell [MATH: {\color{red}\square},] we swap to state [MATH: q_0,] write down [MATH: 0] into the cell, and move right. So, [MATH: \delta(q_1,\square) = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(q_0,0,R)}.]

  • Consider the cell at the intersection of row [MATH: q_0] and column [MATH: {\color{red}1}.] In the diagram, there are no arrows from [MATH: q_0] with a label of the form [MATH: 0] This means that being in state [MATH: q_0] and observing symbol [MATH: {\color{red}1}] in a cell, the machine gets stuck. So, [MATH: \delta(q_0,1)] is undefined and we write [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-}] into the transition table.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A Turing machine is similar to a deterministic finite automaton. However, it is not finite because it has an associated tape of infinite length split into cells, and data may be read and written to the tape, one cell at a time. It is a universal machine, acting as an acceptor or a transducer depending on the setup.

Content:
More formally, a Turing machine is a seven-tuple of the form [MATH: T=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,q_1,q_0,\square,\delta),] where

Content:
- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states,
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols,
- [MATH: \Gamma] is a finite set of tape symbols with [MATH: \Sigma \subseteq \Gamma,]
- [MATH: q_1 \in Q] is the start state,
- [MATH: q_0] is the final or accepting state,
- [MATH: \square \in \Gamma \setminus \Sigma] is the blank cell symbol, representing an empty cell on the tape, and
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta : Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L,R\}.]

Content:
The function [MATH: \delta] takes the current state [MATH: q] and current tape symbol [MATH: X] and returns a state [MATH: q,] a tape symbol [MATH: Y,] and a direction [MATH: D,] either left ([MATH: L]) or right ([MATH: R]).

Content:
Before discussing the tape's mechanics, let's ensure we can understand Turing machine diagrams and transition tables.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Representing Turing Machines Using Transition Diagrams and Tables

Content:
We can visualize a Turing machine as a directed graph, just like for finite automata, where

Content:
- vertices represent the states,
- edges, each labeled with a state, a tape symbol, and a direction, represent transitions from one state to another,
- the start state is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to,] and
- the final state is circled by a double line.

Content:
For example, shown below is a diagram representing the Turing machine with states [MATH: Q=\{q_1,q_2,q_0\},] input symbols [MATH: \{0,1\},] tape symbols [MATH: \{0,1, \square\},] blank cell symbol [MATH: \square,] start state [MATH: q_1,] and final state [MATH: q_0.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/04682b96a1494b0d5328124b21c74e1a]

Content:
On a transition diagram representing a Turing machine, an edge from state [MATH: \color{blue}q] to state [MATH: p] labeled "[MATH: {\color{blue}X}/Y,D]" means that
[MATH: \delta({\color{blue}q},{\color{blue}X}) = (p,Y,D).]

Content:
For instance, the edge from [MATH: \color{red}q_1] to [MATH: q_2] in the Turing machine above is labeled "[MATH: {\color{red}1}/0,R]".
This means that
[MATH: \delta({\color{blue}q_1},{\color{blue}1}) = (q_2,0,R).]
This can be interpreted as follows: if the machine in state [MATH: {\color{blue}q_1}] observes symbol [MATH: {\color{blue}1}] on the tape, it swaps to state [MATH: q_2,] writes [MATH: 0] on the tape, and moves right [MATH: (R).]

Content:
The same machine can be represented using the transition table below.

Content:

Item 3 — Example: Constructing the Transition Table of a Turing Machine Given a Transition Diagram

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/c3a1cab60d57f7ae2e3c0262437952d9]

| [MATH: \to \! q_1] | | [MATH: (q_1,0,L)] | |
| [MATH: \ast \: q_0] | [MATH: -] | | [MATH: -] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A Turing machine is a seven-tuple of the form [MATH: T = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, q_1, q_0, \square, \delta),] where

- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states,
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols,
- [MATH: \Gamma] is a finite set of tape symbols with [MATH: \Sigma \subseteq \Gamma,]
- [MATH: q_1 \in Q] is the start state,
- [MATH: q_0] is the final or accepting state,
- [MATH: \square \in \Gamma \setminus \Sigma] is the blank cell symbol, and
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta: Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{ L, R \}.]

The arguments of [MATH: \delta] are a state and a tape symbol currently scanned by the tape head. The function returns a new state, a new tape symbol replacing the old symbol in the scanned cell, and the direction in which the head moves ([MATH: L] stands for "left" and [MATH: R] stands for "right").

With that in mind, let's examine our diagram.

- Consider the cell at the intersection of row [MATH: q_1] and column [MATH: {\color{red}0}.] In the diagram, this corresponds to the loop from [MATH: q_1] to [MATH: q_1,] labeled by [MATH: {\color{red}0}/1,L.]

[IMG: /graphics/680b46a4dfdb5afd5852adb0c1db7d1a]

This means that being in state [MATH: q_1] and observing symbol [MATH: {\color{red}0}] in a cell, we stay in state [MATH: q_1,] write down [MATH: 1] into the cell, and move left. So,
[MATH: \delta(q_1,0) = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(q_1,1,L)}.]

- Consider the cell at the intersection of row [MATH: q_1] and column [MATH: {\color{red}\square}.] In the diagram, this corresponds to the arrow from [MATH: q_1] to [MATH: q_0,] labeled by [MATH: {\color{red}\square}/0,R.]

[IMG: /graphics/cc37db4f7e97da4722ed695a3dc1f38a]

This means that being in state [MATH: q_1] and observing an empty cell [MATH: {\color{red}\square},] we swap to state [MATH: q_0,] write down [MATH: 0] into the cell, and move right. So,
[MATH: \delta(q_1,\square) = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(q_0,0,R)}.]
- Consider the cell at the intersection of row [MATH: q_0] and column [MATH: {\color{red}1}.] In the diagram, there are no arrows from [MATH: q_0] with a label of the form [MATH: 0] This means that being in state [MATH: q_0] and observing symbol [MATH: {\color{red}1}] in a cell, the machine gets stuck. So, [MATH: \delta(q_0,1)] is undefined and we write [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-}] into the transition table.

Finally, the transition table of the Turing machine takes on the following form:

| [MATH: \Large _{Q} \!\backslash\! ^{\Gamma}] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \square] |
| [MATH: \to \! q_1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(q_1,1,L)}] | [MATH: (q_1,0,L)] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(q_0,0,R)}] |
| [MATH: \ast \: q_0] | [MATH: -] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-}] | [MATH: -] |
